steps.title: 1. Problem analysis and curriculum links
steps.description:
We are asked to evaluate the definite integral
  ∫₀^{π/8} x·sin(2x) dx.
This is an INTEGRATION—CONTINUED task: the integrand is a product of a polynomial (x) and a trigonometric function (sin(2x)), so integration by parts is the standard technique listed in the syllabus.
steps.hints: Recognise that integration by parts is triggered whenever the integrand is a product f(x)·g(x) where one factor becomes simpler after differentiation.

steps.title: 2. Choose the parts for the IBP formula
steps.description:
Integration-by-parts formula (single variable): ∫ u dv = u·v − ∫ v du.
Take
  u = x          (easy to differentiate ⇒ du = dx)
  dv = sin(2x) dx  (easy to integrate ⇒ v = −½ cos(2x)).
steps.hints: Pick u so that its derivative simplifies the product, and pick dv so that v is easy to find.

steps.title: 3. Apply the integration-by-parts formula (indefinite integral first)
steps.description:
∫ x·sin(2x) dx = u·v − ∫ v du
                 = x(−½ cos(2x)) − ∫ (−½ cos(2x)) dx
                 = −½ x cos(2x) + ½ ∫ cos(2x) dx.
Now integrate cos(2x):
  ∫ cos(2x) dx = ½ sin(2x).
Therefore
  ∫ x·sin(2x) dx = −½ x cos(2x) + ½·½ sin(2x) + C
                 = −½ x cos(2x) + ¼ sin(2x) + C.
steps.hints: After IBP you usually need one more basic integral; here it is ∫ cos(2x).

steps.title: 4. Convert to the required definite integral
steps.description:
Evaluate F(x)= −½ x cos(2x) + ¼ sin(2x) at the limits 0 and π/8.
Upper limit  x = π/8:
  cos(2x)=cos(π/4)=√2/2,
  sin(2x)=sin(π/4)=√2/2.
F(π/8) = −½ (π/8)(√2/2) + ¼(√2/2)
       = − (π√2)/32 + √2/8.
Lower limit  x=0:
  F(0)=0.
Hence the definite integral equals F(π/8) − F(0).
steps.hints: Trigonometric values at π/4 are standard exact numbers (√2/2).

steps.title: 6. (Optional) Numerical check
steps.description:
√2 ≈ 1.41421356 and 4 − π ≈ 0.858407.
Integral ≈ (1.41421356)(0.858407)/32 ≈ 0.0379.
A quick graph or a numerical integral confirms the magnitude, providing confidence in the analytic result.
steps.hints: A sanity-check with technology or rough area estimation is always good practice.
